parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Thread (TH)**
> 
> Thread (TH) makes school uniforms in country Z. It was set up four years ago by Mariam, who had spent nine years working as a buyer for a large clothing retailer.
> 
> While working as a buyer, Mariam noticed that schools in her region were paying high prices for uniforms imported from overseas. She believed the same garments could be made locally for far less. She left her job, invested \$30,000 of her own savings, and formed a partnership with her sister, who contributed a further \$20,000.
> 
> Mariam rented a small factory unit and bought twelve industrial sewing machines. She recruited 60 workers from the local area, most of whom had never used industrial equipment before, and trained them herself over three months. She also negotiated directly with a fabric mill in a neighbouring country, cutting out the wholesalers that her competitors use.
> 
> TH now sells a hard-wearing cotton blend that Mariam developed with the mill. Schools report that the uniforms last around a year longer than the imported ones they replaced.
> 
> **Table 1.1: TH selected data**
> 
> | Revenue in year 1 (\$) | 180,000 |
> |---|---|
> | Revenue in year 4 (\$) | 940,000 |
> | Number of schools supplied | 34 |
> | TH price compared with imported uniforms | 25% lower |
> 
> Mariam is now considering whether TH should begin supplying schools in a neighbouring region.

Analyse **two** ways in which Mariam has carried out the role of an entrepreneur at TH.
parts.solution_md:
One way Mariam has acted as an entrepreneur is by spotting an opportunity in the market **[K]**. While working as a buyer she noticed that schools in her region were paying high prices for imported uniforms, and her experience of the clothing trade told her the same garments could be produced locally for much less **[Ap]**. By setting TH's prices 25% below the imported alternatives, she gave schools a clear financial reason to change supplier, which explains why TH has won orders from 34 schools in only four years **[An]**. Those customers have lifted revenue from \$180,000 to \$940,000, giving TH the income it needs to fund further growth **[An]** A second way is by organising the factors of production **[K]**. Mariam rented a factory unit, bought twelve industrial sewing machines and recruited 60 local workers, most of whom had never used this kind of equipment before **[Ap]**. By training them herself over three months instead of paying to attract experienced machinists from rival firms, she kept TH's wage costs lower than a competitor would face, which is part of the reason TH can undercut imported uniforms and still make a profit **[An]**. Having a workforce she has trained also means TH can raise output fairly quickly when new schools place orders, so Mariam can take on customers in the neighbouring region without long delays that might send those schools to a competitor instead **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

- The answer makes a basic attempt to explain the causes, impacts or consequences of **one** point | | | | > > **Indicative content** > > - Entrepreneurs identify unmet needs that existing firms have overlooked; Mariam's nine years as a buyer gave her knowledge of both what schools were paying and what garments actually cost to produce, so she could judge that a local manufacturer would be viable where others had not - without that insight TH would not exist, and the speed of its growth to 34 schools suggests the gap she identified was real rather than imagined > - Entrepreneurs accept personal financial risk that others are unwilling to take; Mariam gave up a secure salaried job and committed \$30,000 of her own savings, with her sister adding \$20,000 as a partner - if TH had failed, both would have lost their investment, and it was this willingness to risk their own money that allowed TH to start trading at all when no lender would have backed an untested business > - Entrepreneurs bring together land, labour and capital and organise them into a working business; Mariam secured the factory unit, bought the twelve sewing machines and built a workforce of 60 from people with no industrial experience, training them personally - decisions of this kind determine whether a business can actually produce at the cost and quality its market requires > - Entrepreneurs innovate in how they produce and supply, not only in what they sell; by negotiating directly with the fabric mill Mariam removed the wholesalers her competitors rely on, lowering TH's input costs, and by developing a longer-lasting cotton blend she gave schools a reason to buy from TH beyond price alone - making TH harder to displace if a rival ever matches its prices > > Accept any other valid response.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Lattice (LT)**
> 
> Lattice (LT) is a private limited company based in country Y. It was founded fourteen years ago and now employs 320 people. LT develops software that helps delivery companies plan their routes.
> 
> Almost all of LT's income comes from a single product, RouteMaster, which was launched eleven years ago. Two competitors have released newer route-planning software in the past eighteen months, and several of LT's customers have asked why RouteMaster has changed so little.
> 
> **Table 1.1: LT selected data**
> 
> | Revenue in 2025 (\$m) | 24 |
> |---|---|
> | Share of revenue from RouteMaster (%) | 78 |
> | Labour turnover, software developers (%) | 22 |
> | Industry average labour turnover (%) | 14 |
> 
> Several of LT's software developers have suggested ideas for new products, but they have no time to work on them because they are fully occupied maintaining RouteMaster for existing customers.
> 
> LT's Managing Director, Anika, wants to encourage intrapreneurship. She has proposed that every developer is given one day each fortnight to work on their own project, and that LT sets aside an annual fund of \$200,000 to develop the most promising employee ideas.
> 
> LT's Finance Director disagrees. He estimates that the lost development time would cost LT around \$900,000 each year, and points out that most employee ideas never become products that customers will pay for.

Analyse **two** benefits to LT of encouraging intrapreneurship among its employees.
parts.solution_md:
One benefit is that intrapreneurship could help LT develop new products **[K]**. At the moment 78% of LT's revenue comes from RouteMaster, a product launched eleven years ago, and two competitors have released newer software in the past eighteen months **[Ap]**. Giving developers one day each fortnight to work on their own ideas would allow LT to test far more concepts than it does now, without the cost of hiring an outside development team **[An]**. If even one of these ideas became a product that customers were willing to buy, LT would earn income from a second source, so a future fall in RouteMaster sales would no longer put the whole business at risk **[An]** A second benefit is that intrapreneurship should improve staff retention **[K]**. Labour turnover among LT's software developers is 22%, which is much higher than the industry average of 14% **[Ap]**. Developers who are trusted to work on their own projects are likely to find their work more interesting and feel their ideas are valued, which makes them less willing to leave for a competitor **[An]**. Lower turnover would cut the money LT spends on recruiting and training replacements, and would keep hold of experienced staff who already understand how RouteMaster is built, meaning that customer requests are dealt with more quickly than they would be by a constant stream of new employees **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

- The answer links **one** relevant point to the business in the case study | **2 marks**

- The answer makes a basic attempt to explain the causes, impacts or consequences of **one** point | | | | > > **Indicative content** > > - LT depends heavily on one ageing product, with 78% of its \$24m revenue coming from RouteMaster; intrapreneurship gives LT a low-cost route to a wider product range because the ideas come from employees who already understand the delivery market, so LT could spread its risk without the expense of acquiring another software business or recruiting a separate research team > - Employees who are given responsibility for their own projects gain greater job satisfaction and a sense of achievement, which are powerful non-financial motivators; with developer turnover running at 22% against an industry average of 14%, LT is losing staff faster than its rivals, and every departure takes away knowledge of how RouteMaster works - reducing turnover protects that knowledge as well as cutting recruitment costs > - Two competitors have launched newer software within eighteen months and customers are already questioning why RouteMaster has changed so little; intrapreneurship allows LT to respond much faster than a traditional development process would, because ideas can be trialled by existing staff rather than waiting for board approval of a large formal project - speed matters in a market where customers can switch to a rival's product > - Intrapreneurship carries less risk for LT than external innovation, because the employees generating ideas already know the customers, the technology and the constraints of the business; ideas that would obviously not work are filtered out early by people with practical experience, so the \$200,000 fund is more likely to be spent on concepts with a genuine chance of reaching the market > > Accept any other valid response.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Kiln (KL)**
> 
> Priya worked for twelve years as a secondary school art teacher in country X. She has always made handmade ceramic tableware in her spare time and sells it at local craft markets. Last year she decided to leave teaching and set up Kiln (KL) as a sole trader, producing handmade plates, bowls and mugs to sell to homeware shops.
> 
> Priya has \$18,000 in personal savings. She estimates that KL needs \$45,000 before it can begin trading, as shown in Table 1.1. She approached two banks for a loan. Both refused, saying that KL has no trading record and no assets to offer as security.
> 
> **Table 1.1: KL estimated start-up costs**
> 
> | **Item** | **Cost (\$)** |
> |---|---|
> | Industrial kiln | 20,000 |
> | Workshop equipment and tools | 9,000 |
> | First three months' rent on workshop | 8,500 |
> | Raw materials (clay and glazes) | 5,000 |
> | Safety certification and licences | 2,500 |
> | **Total** | **45,000** |
> 
> The homeware market in country X is dominated by three established manufacturers. The largest holds 40% of the market and supplies plates to retailers at \$12 each. Priya has calculated that KL's cost of making one plate is \$9.
> 
> Before KL can begin production, its workshop must pass a safety inspection. Priya has been told that the certification process usually takes about four months.
> 
> Priya is confident about the quality of her designs. However, she has no experience of pricing, managing cash flow or negotiating with suppliers. A friend has advised her to write a business plan before going any further.

Analyse **two** barriers to entrepreneurship faced by Priya.
parts.solution_md:
One barrier Priya faces is a lack of finance **[K]**. KL needs \$45,000 to begin trading but Priya has only \$18,000 in savings, and both banks have refused to lend because KL has no trading record **[Ap]**. This leaves a shortfall of \$27,000, so Priya may have to buy a smaller or second-hand kiln and cut back on raw materials, which would reduce the number of items KL can produce each month **[An]**. Producing fewer items means lower revenue at a time when Priya must still pay the \$8,500 workshop rent, so KL could run out of cash before it has built up a regular group of customers **[An]** A second barrier is strong competition from established manufacturers **[K]**. Three firms already dominate the homeware market in country X, and the largest supplies plates to retailers at \$12 each while KL's cost of making one plate is \$9 **[Ap]**. This leaves Priya a margin of only \$3 per plate if she matches the market price, which is very little to cover her rent and other fixed costs **[An]**. If she charges more than \$12 to protect her margin, retailers may simply buy from the larger manufacturers instead, so KL could struggle to win enough orders to survive its first year **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

- The answer clearly explains the causes, impacts or consequences of **one** point | | | | > | **1** | **1 mark**

- The answer shows knowledge of **one** relevant point that answers the question | **1 mark**

- The answer links **one** relevant point to the business in the case study | **2 marks**

- The answer makes a basic attempt to explain the causes, impacts or consequences of **two** points. | > | **1 mark**

- The answer makes a basic attempt to explain the causes, impacts or consequences of **one** point | | | | > > **Indicative content** > > - Priya cannot raise the capital KL needs to start trading; with \$18,000 of savings against \$45,000 of start-up costs, and two banks unwilling to lend to a business with no trading history, she faces a funding gap of \$27,000 - she may be forced to delay the launch while she saves more, and every month of delay is a month in which the established manufacturers strengthen their hold on the retailers KL hopes to supply > - The homeware market in country X is already dominated by three established manufacturers, the largest of which holds 40% of the market and can supply plates at \$12; larger producers benefit from economies of scale that Priya cannot match as a sole trader making items by hand, so KL will find it difficult to compete on price and must instead persuade retailers that its handmade quality justifies a higher one - a much harder sell to buyers who compare on cost > - Priya has strong design skills but no experience of pricing, cash flow management or negotiating with suppliers; running KL requires all of these at once, and a mistake in any one of them is costly - if she agrees poor payment terms with a clay supplier, for example, KL could be paying for materials before its own customers have paid, creating a cash shortage even if the business is winning orders > - The four-month wait for safety certification means KL cannot produce or sell anything for a third of a year, while the \$2,500 fee must be paid up front from savings Priya has already stretched; during this period she has no revenue at all but is still committed to workshop rent, which reduces the capital available to buy raw materials once KL is finally allowed to begin trading > > Accept any other valid response.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **The Shop (TS) **
> 
> Thomas worked for 30 years as a manager of a factory. Although he was very good at his job, he was recently made redundant.
> 
> Thomas always wanted to open a shop. He thinks he has the qualities an entrepreneur is likely to need for success. He has undertaken some primary market research to identify possible opportunities in city X where he lives (see Fig. 1.1).
> 
> ![Pie chart showing shop preference: sandwich shop 25%, bakery shop 20%, coffee and grocery shops 15% each, electronics and butcher shops 10% each, clothes shop 5%.](assets/001-pie-chart-showing-shop-preference-sandwich-shop-.png)
> 
> **Fig. 1.1: Market research**
> 
> Thomas now needs to make a decision about which type of shop to open. He has used the data in Fig. 1.1 and some secondary market research to identify two options.
> 
> *Option 1: Coffee shop *
> The coffee shop would provide hot drinks that customers could take away and drink elsewhere. It would also sell some bakery items, such as biscuits and doughnuts. There are four other shops selling takeaway hot drinks and bakery items in the city, as well as five cafés. Thomas thinks that the profit margin would be 6% to 8%.
> 
> *Option 2: Sandwich shop *
> The sandwich shop would make sandwiches using job production. Customers can choose from a range of sandwich fillings, as well as cold drinks and snacks. There is only one competitor in the city. It is a well-known international franchise that spends a lot of money on promotion. Thomas thinks that the profit margin would be 10% to 15%.

Recommend which of the two options Thomas should choose for his new shop. Justify your recommendation.
parts.solution_md:
Thomas could open a coffee shop, which targets two market segments and could attract up to 35% of potential customers in city X **[K] [Ap]**. The combination of hot drinks and bakery items creates synergy, as both tend to appeal to similar customers looking for a quick snack **[An]**. The presence of four takeaway shops and five cafés in the city **[Ap]** also confirms that demand already exists for this type of service **[An]**. However, competing against nine existing businesses would make it very difficult for Thomas to establish a USP, and the profit margin of only 6–8% **[Ap]** leaves very little room for a new business to absorb its start-up costs **[E]**

Alternatively, Thomas could open a sandwich shop. The sandwich market is the largest single segment **[K]** in city X at 25%, and there is only one competitor - an international franchise **[Ap]**. By using job production, Thomas could offer fully customised sandwiches, giving him a clear, attractive USP over the franchise, which relies on standardised production methods **[An]**. The profit margin of 10–15% is also significantly higher than Option 1. However, the franchise spends heavily on promotion, so Thomas may struggle to attract customers initially, as many people in city X may already be loyal to the existing brand **[E]**

I recommend that Thomas opens a sandwich shop **[E]**. Although the coffee shop targets a larger share of the market overall, the nine competitors would make it very hard for a new business to survive on a margin of only 6–8% **[Ap]**. The sandwich shop has far less competition and a higher profit margin, making it much more likely that Thomas can reach break-even and build a sustainable business **[E]**. The franchise's promotional spending is a challenge, but Thomas's use of job production gives him a genuine advantage that a large, standardised franchise cannot easily replicate **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge and application, analysis and evaluation
> - A full-mark answer will include
> 
>   - Strong knowledge applied to the business context or question stem throughout
>   - Detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning
>   - Evaluation of relevant issues which leads to a conclusion supported by strong reasoning
>   - The importance of at least two points must be identified and analysed
> 
> **Knowledge and application**
> 
> | **Mark** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|
> | **4** | - Shows understanding of both options in context |
> | **3** | - Shows understanding of one option in context |
> | **2** | - Shows knowledge of both options |
> | **1** | - Shows knowledge of one option |
> 
> **Analysis and evaluation**
> 
> | **Mark** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|
> | **8** | - Justified recommendation with developed weighing of key arguments in business context |
> | **7** | - Justified recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **6** | - Developed recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **5** | - An evaluative statement or recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **4** | - Argument based on two challenges in context |
> | **3** | - Argument based on one challenge in context |
> | **2** | - Analysis of two options |
> | **1** | - Analysis of one option |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Option 1 (coffee shop) targets two market segments from the research, meaning Thomas could potentially attract 35% of the market. The combination of hot drinks and bakery items creates synergy, as both tend to appeal to similar customers, and the presence of four takeaway shops and five cafés in the city confirms that demand already exists.
> - However, competing against nine existing businesses would make it very difficult for Thomas to establish a USP, and the profit margin of only 6–8% leaves little room for error in a new business
> - Option 2 (sandwich shop) targets 25% of the market — the largest single segment — with only one competitor. Using job production to make customised sandwiches would give Thomas a clear USP over the international franchise, which uses standardised production and cannot easily match a personalised service. The profit margin of 10–15% is significantly higher than Option 1
> - However, the franchise competitor spends heavily on promotion, which could make it difficult for Thomas to attract customers initially, as many people in city X may already have strong brand loyalty to the franchise.
> - The sandwich shop is the stronger recommendation because the combination of higher profit margin, lower competition, and a clear USP through job production gives Thomas a more realistic chance of building a sustainable business. The coffee shop reaches a larger overall market share but the intense competition (nine rivals) and low profit margin make survival much harder for a start-up with no established reputation.
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problem_md: Explain **two **reasons why many new businesses fail in their first year of operation.
parts.solution_md:
One reason many new businesses fail in their first year is a lack of finance** [1]**. A new business may struggle to pay for premises, stock, and employees for several months before revenue is high enough to cover costs **[1]**

A second reason is poor or inadequate market research **[1]**. If the entrepreneur misjudges customer demand the business cannot may not be able to cover its costs and is unlikely to survive its first year **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires the clear identification of two reasons (AO1), each supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded up to 2 marks
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - The product or service is not wanted by enough consumers
> - Lack of business or management experience
> - Insufficient finance to sustain early operations
> - Poor or inadequate market research
> - An unexpected change in economic conditions
> - A strong competitive reaction from established businesses
> 
> AO2
> 
> - If the product has no real demand, sales will be too low to cover costs and the business will be unable to survive
> - Without experience, owners are likely to make poor decisions around pricing, staffing, or cash flow, which can quickly threaten the business's survival
> - A new business may have to fund its operations for months before revenue is sufficient to cover costs, and without enough capital it will run out of cash
> - Flawed market research produces inaccurate information about customer demand, meaning the business may invest in a product or service that the market does not actually want
> - A downturn in the economy may cause consumers to cut spending, reducing sales below the level needed for the business to break even
> - Established competitors may respond by cutting prices or increasing advertising, making it very difficult for a new business to attract enough customers

One quality of a successful entrepreneur is a willingness to take risks **[1]**. An entrepreneur must be prepared to invest their own time and money into a business idea with no guarantee of success **[1]**. An entrepreneur is also self-motivated and determined **[1]**. Building a business involves setbacks and obstacles, so a successful entrepreneur must be able to persist and adapt after failure is essential **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires the clear identification of two entrepreneurial qualities (AO1), each supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded up to 2 marks
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Ability to identify and develop innovative business proposals/projects / solve problems
> - Self-confident – energetic and driven
> - Self-motivated and multi-skilled
> - Ability to lead, inspire and motivate others
> - Good communicator/persuasive
> - Visionary
> - Creative
> - Passionate, resolute, optimistic
> - Future-centric
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A willingness to take risks allows an entrepreneur to commit personal capital to an untested business idea, essential for bringing new products or services to market
> - Being self-motivated and determined means an entrepreneur can persist through early setbacks such as low sales or cash flow problems, adapting their approach rather than giving up
> - Strong leadership and communication skills enable an entrepreneur to attract investors, recruit talented employees and build customer loyalty
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you do more than simply list qualities - the command word is "explain", so you need to develop each point by stating why or how that quality helps an entrepreneur succeed. A common mistake is to name several qualities without explaining any of them, which limits you to just 1 mark. Structure your answer clearly: identify the quality, then explain its importance. Two well-explained qualities will score much better than a long list of undeveloped ones.

**[4 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Clever Televisions (CTV) **
> 
> CTV is a public limited company that produces and sells televisions. It has been operating in country A for 30 years. CTV owns 3 factories and has over 100 employees. CTV’s factories use a combination of capital and skilled labour to produce the televisions. The leadership style in all the factories is autocratic. Employees’ pay is based on time worked each week.
> 
> The CTV brand is known for high‑quality and reliability. It targets high‑income customers. CTV uses price skimming when it launches a new product.
> 
> In total, 6 million televisions were sold in country A in 2019. Table 2.1 shows market growth data.
> 
> **Table 2.1: Television sales in country A**
> 
> | **Year** | **Market growth** |
> |---|---|
> | 2020 | +2% |
> | 2021 | +1% |
> | 2022 | –3% (forecast) |
> 
> The market for televisions in country A is very competitive, and the business environment is dynamic. CTV plans to introduce a lower-priced television brand to appeal to the mass market. This brand will be known as STV.
> 
> CTV has decided to introduce automation into one of its factories to produce the STV televisions. This will lead to redundancies in that factory.
> 
> The employees in the other two factories are concerned they might also face redundancy and so motivation is currently low. The Human Resources Director recommends that CTV should find ways in which employees can participate in the management and control of the business.

Explain what is meant by ‘the business environment is dynamic’.
parts.solution_md:
The business environment refers to the external factors outside a business's control that affect how it operates, such as competition, economic conditions, and market trends **[1]**. Dynamic means these factors are always changing, and businesses must adapt their strategies in response **[1]**. For CTV, the television market in country A illustrates this - market growth has declined from +2% in 2020 to a forecast of –3% in 2022, and rising competition has forced CTV to respond by launching the new lower-priced STV brand **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - External factors that affect how a business operates, such as economic conditions, competition, technology and market trends
> - Dynamic means these external factors are constantly changing rather than remaining stable or predictable
> - A dynamic environment requires businesses to adapt their strategies in response to shifting conditions
> 
> AO2
> 
> - For CTV, the television market in country A illustrates this — market growth has declined from +2% in 2020 to a forecast of –3% in 2022, showing that conditions are changing and forcing CTV to respond by launching the lower-priced STV brand
> - The increasingly competitive television market means CTV cannot rely on its existing strategy and must adapt, for example by introducing automation and targeting the mass market with STV
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Break the phrase into its two components - 'business environment' and 'dynamic' - and explain each separately. Many students only define one part and miss out on a mark. After defining both parts, give a brief example or further development to secure the third mark. For instance, you could mention that new competitors may enter the market, technology may change, or consumer tastes may shift. Make sure your example clearly links back to the idea of the external environment changing.

**[3 marks]**

parts.problem_md: Discuss the possible challenges for an entrepreneur in starting a new business selling only vegetarian food products.
parts.solution_md:
An entrepreneur is a person who takes on financial risk to start and run a business **[K]**. Opening a business selling only vegetarian food products has some good opportunities, but there are also challenges of operating in such a niche market to consider **[Ap]**

One challenge is the higher cost of vegetarian ingredients. As a new business, the entrepreneur will not benefit from economies of scale, so costs per unit will be higher than for larger competitors **[K] [Ap]**. This means the entrepreneur must either charge higher prices and risk losing customers or accept lower profit margins, both of which make it harder to survive in the early months **[An]**

A second challenge is that vegetarian food may be a trend rather than a permanent change in consumer behaviour **[K]**. If demand slows or falls, a business that only sells vegetarian products cannot easily switch to meat or fish-based products **[Ap]**, which could lead to falling sales and business failure **[An]**

Overall, the biggest long-term challenge is competition **[E]**. In the short term, entering a growing market early is an advantage. However, as the market gets bigger, larger food businesses with more money and better supply chains will enter, making it harder for a small new business to compete on price or promotion **[An]**. The entrepreneur's best chance of success is to build a loyal customer base and a strong brand quickly, before this competition arrives **[E]**

A new business in this sector can target health-conscious consumers and those adopting plant-based diets as a permanent lifestyle choice. However, as the market grows, it will attract larger, well-funded competitors with greater economies of scale, making it progressively harder for a small new entrant to compete on price

A vegetarian food start-up will not yet benefit from bulk purchasing or economies of scale, meaning its prices may be higher than those of established rivals. parts.problem_md: Analyse **two** ways marketing could be used to add value to a product.
parts.solution_md:
One way marketing can add value is by building a strong brand through advertising **[K]**. When a business spends money on advertising to create a well-known and trusted brand image, customers begin to see the product as worth more than similar products from less well-known competitors **[An]**. For example, a clothing brand with a strong image can charge a higher price than an unbranded item that costs roughly the same to make **[Ap]**. This widens the gap between the selling price and the cost of production, which increases the added value the business creates **[An]** Another way marketing can add value is by promoting a clear unique selling point (USP) **[K]**. If a business highlights something that makes its product different from competitors, such as an eco-friendly ingredient or an exclusive feature **[Ap]**, customers who care about this difference are often willing to pay a higher price for it. This means the business can increase its selling price without a large rise in production costs, which increases added value **[An]**. As word spreads about this unique feature, the business may also attract new customers who specifically want that benefit, further growing sales at these higher, more profitable prices **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to a business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

It has a joint venture with a restaurant close to the hotel where SH’s customers receive a discount on their food and drink. The hotel advertises the restaurant on social media and the restaurant advertises the hotel on its menu. > > Tia is one of the managers of SH. She has an autocratic leadership style and is responsible for the cleaners and marketing employees. > > The directors of SH aim to increase the value added to the service that SH provides. Recommend how SH could increase the value added to its service. Justify your recommendation.
parts.solution_md:
SH could add its own restaurant to increase value added **[K]**. Currently, SH relies on a joint venture with a nearby restaurant **[Ap]**, meaning all food and drink revenue goes to another business **[An]**. If SH opened its own restaurant, guests would receive more as part of their stay, increasing the perceived value of the hotel and allowing SH to charge a higher room rate **[An]**. However, setting up a restaurant would require significant investment in equipment and the recruitment of new staff with catering skills, increasing costs considerably in the short term **[E]**

SH could also use its sea views as a USP and invest in stronger branding **[K]**. The hotel already benefits from good views and a popular tourist location, but off-peak occupancy is only 45% **[Ap]**, suggesting many potential guests are not aware of SH or are choosing competitors instead. By promoting the sea views more strongly through social media, SH could differentiate itself and justify charging a higher price **[An]**. However, other hotels in the same tourist area may also offer sea views, which could limit how much SH is able to stand out from its competitors on this basis alone **[E]**

I recommend that SH add its own restaurant **[E]**. Although the start-up costs are a risk, the restaurant would create an entirely new revenue stream from food and drink, something that stronger branding cannot do. Branding would mainly affect how many rooms are sold, but SH already sells 95% of its rooms in the peak season **[Ap]**, leaving little room to grow through attracting more guests **[E]**. A restaurant would allow SH to earn more from the guests it already has, making it the more effective and sustainable way to increase value added in the long run **[E]**

> 
> - Man-made assets used to produce goods or services, such as machinery, factories, or vehicles
> - Manufactured resources that are used in the production process rather than being consumed directly, for example tools or equipment
> - Human-created physical or financial resources used by a business to produce output
> 
> A clear, correct definition earns 2 marks. A partial, vague or unfocused definition earns 1 mark

> **[exam-tip]**
> When asked to define a term, always aim to give a precise meaning first and then support it with a brief example. Many students lose a mark by only providing an example (e.g. "machinery") without explaining the broader meaning of the term. Make sure your definition distinguishes capital from other factors of production - emphasise that it is a non-human, man-made resource rather than a natural or human resource.

**[2 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Great Resources (GR) **
> 
> GR is a business partnership that creates educational resources. It sells direct to schools and teachers via its own website.
> 
> Sanjay, Rukmal and Boris are entrepreneurial teachers who formed the GR partnership. One year ago, they identified a gap in the market to supply interactive, digital resources. GR’s website is subscription only. An online marketing campaign, which used penetration pricing, attracted 250 subscribers in the first six months of operation. The start-up costs were financed with a \$5000 bank overdraft, which is GR’s only debt.
> 
> Reviews for GR’s products in teaching journals are positive but cash flow is poor. Many customers have taken advantage of a recent sales promotion for one month’s free membership and posted positive reviews. Unfortunately, few have then taken out a regular subscription.
> 
> As revenue has not increased as much as the entrepreneurs had hoped, they must now consider alternative promotion methods. They have researched possible promotion methods and decided to advertise in an educational newspaper. The newspaper has a readership of half a million people.
> 
> Expert Materials (EM) is a large national company that also advertises in the newspaper. EM is GR’s closest competitor. The EM brand is well-known and trusted in the educational resources market. Table 1.1 shows some marketing data.
> 
> **Table 1.1 Marketing data**
> 
> |   | GR | EM | Total market |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Revenue (\$000) | 15 | 300 | 500 |
> | Number of customers | 300 | 5000 | 7000 |
> | Annual advertising spend (\$000) | 7.5 | 45 | 60 |

Identify **one **barrier to entrepreneurship.
parts.solution_md:
Lack of available finance **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Identify requires you to name or state a relevant barrier; no further explanation is needed.
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Lack of a strategic plan
> - Fear of failure
> - Strong rules and regulations
> - Lack of capacity
> 
> Accept other valid responses.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question asks you to "identify", a brief, clear statement is all that is required - you do not need to explain or justify your answer. Make sure you give only the number of points asked for; here, just one barrier is needed. Common barriers to entrepreneurship include financial constraints, regulatory hurdles and fear of failure. Avoid vague responses such as "it is difficult" - be specific about the type of barrier.

**[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Designer Clothing (DC)**
> 
> DC is a medium-sized private limited company. It has been trading for 10 years. DC makes luxury dresses for women using job production methods. DC has an excellent reputation for quality. A DC designer has a meeting with every customer to design a dress that satisfies the customer’s individual needs, including choice of fabric and colour. Cost-based pricing is used with 50% added to the average cost of each dress.
> 
> DC’s employees are highly skilled and paid hourly rates (a time-based method). Ikram, one of the designers, has just had a meeting with a new customer, Lydia. Lydia wants Ikram to design and make a new dress for her. Ikram has worked out the production data shown in Table 2.1 for the dress.
> 
> **Table 2.1: Production data for the dress for Lydia**
> 
> | Production time | 20 hours |
> |---|---|
> | Hourly rate | \$10 |
> | Material costs | \$250 |
> | Indirect cost allocation | \$25 |
> | Other costs such as packaging | \$25 |
> 
> Jenny, the Managing Director, wants to use DC’s excellent reputation and move into a new market. Jenny wants to create a new range of DC branded trousers for women. Jenny has developed some elements of a marketing mix for the new trousers:
> 
> - Product: quality trousers aimed at women aged 25–50
> - Distribution channel: sold in large shops
> - Promotion: branded with the DC logo
> 
> Jenny will develop a business plan when she receives the market research report, which includes feedback from a focus group. Jenny thinks that the pricing strategy DC currently uses will not be appropriate for the new trousers.
> 
> The new product range would use a batch production method. The Production Director, Khaleal, has identified the machinery needed for the new production method. Khaleal is worried about the problems that introducing the new production method might cause DC’s employees.

Explain the term ‘business plan’.
parts.solution_md:
A business plan is a document that sets out the objectives and strategies of a business **[1]**. It includes key information such as financial forecasts and details about the target market **[1]**, which Jenny could use to plan how the new DC trousers range will be launched and sold in large shops **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A document that sets out the objectives and strategies of a business **[1]**
> 
> AO2
> 
> - It includes information specific to the business so Jenny could include financial forecasts for the new trousers range and details about the target market of women aged 25–50
> - Can be used to support a loan application. Given DC may need external finance to purchase the machinery. Khaleal has identified for the batch production method a business plan would help secure lending from a bank
> - Can be used to measure the success of a business so Jenny could compare DC's actual trouser sales against the targets set in the plan to assess whether entering the new market has been worthwhile
> - Helps a business plan entry into a new market. Jenny will use the market research report and focus group findings to inform the plan before committing to launching the new trouser range
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When asked to explain a business term, always start with a clear definition to secure the AO1 knowledge mark. Then develop your answer with relevant detail or examples to earn the AO2 application marks. Many students lose marks by only providing a definition without any further development. Make sure you go beyond simply stating what a business plan is – explain what it contains or how it is used, ideally linking to the context of the case study (e.g. Jenny developing a business plan for the new trousers range).

**[3 marks]**
